newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN oil monitors go to Iraq but deal still delayed.
newsitem.headline: UN oil monitors go to Iraq but deal still delayed.

text.p: An advance team of three inspectors from the Dutch-based Saybolt firm has gone to Iraq after all although implementation of an oil-for-food plan is still delayed, a senior U.N. official said on Wednesday.

U.N. Under-Secretary-General Chinmaya Gharekhan told reporters: "The advance team is on its way to Baghdad. It should have arrived today but it will arrive tomorrow. The advance team of Saybolt should be in Baghdad tomorrow and they will do their job."
Senior U.N. officials and diplomats on Tuesday had said the team postponed its visit because of the unstable conditions in the country's northern regions.
The inspectors were pulled out of Iraq in September when fighting flared in the northern Kurdish provinces and the United Nations delayed implementing an oil-for-food plan.
But Gharekhan indicated their trip to Iraq did not mean quick implementation of the plan since other issues were far from being settled.

For one, he said Iraq has insisted that the Security Council's sanctions committee approve an oil pricing formula before the deal goes into force. Secondly the United Nations is still negotiating with Iraq on demands it finds acceptable concerning freedom of movement of U.N. personnel and the hiring of local employees.

The oil-for-food deal allows Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil over six months, on a renewable basis, to buy food, medicine and other necessities to help offset the effect on ordinary Iraqis of sanctions imposed after Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Arrangements to launch the plan were close to completion when Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into the largely Kurdish-inhabited north of the country at the end of August to back one side in an inter-Kurdish conflict.
